messages.content: i know a song that my mother used to sing, but i have never seen the words written down.
you learned it by hearing her. do you remember the whole song or just part of it?
just the first part. when i sing it, i keep going back to the start.
then the start is the part that is clear in your memory. you could ask your mother to sing more of it if she still knows it.
she can remember it too. i want to write it down while she helps me sing it.
you could ask her to go slowly and sing one short part at a time. write what you hear, then read it back so she can help you check it.
say my plan simply.
you want to write the song while your mother helps you remember the words. ask her for one part at a time, then check what you wrote together.
why read it back instead of only asking her to sing it again?
you may hear the right words but write something different. reading your page to her can help you find that difference.
say that last idea simply.
read your page to her so she can help check the words.
write a story about a child who wants to join a ball game but does not know when to start.

a child watches her brother and cousin playing with a ball. she walks near them and asks whether she can join. her brother says yes, but she does not know where to stand. her cousin says that she can stand near the wall and that the ball will come to her next. she stands there and waits. when the ball comes, she sends it back, and all three keep playing.
make the part about her cousin simple.
her cousin says where she can stand. he says that the ball will come to her next.
say only where she should stand.
her cousin says: stand near the wall. the ball will come to you next.
did asking to join tell her every rule of the game?
no. it let the group know that she wanted to play. she still needed information about where to stand and what to do.
add a question she could ask after the ball comes to her.
should i send it to you or to my brother?
help me ask for a table at a restaurant. there are two of us, and we would like to sit near a window if possible.
could we have a table for two near a window, please?
what if the worker says there is no free table near a window?
you can choose whether another table would work. if the window is only something you would like, rather than something you need, you could say: another table is fine, thank you.
we are happy with another table. now ask if we can have water.
could we have some water, please?
should i ask for two cups or just water?
you can ask for two cups of water if you want to make the number clear. asking for water alone is less specific, though the worker may know it is for both of you from the context.
write the request with the number.
could we have two cups of water, please?
does a table for two mean only two cups can be on it?
no. table for two is about a place for two people to sit. it does not say how many objects can be on the table.
my cousin left a garment at my house. i want to ask how to return it without adding anything about whether they still use it.
you could say: you left a garment at my house. would you like me to bring it when we next meet?
i only want to talk about returning it.
then that message works. it asks about returning the garment without adding more details.
give just the message again.
you left a garment at my house. would you like me to bring it when we next meet?
they say they do not want it back. can i give it to someone else?
ask clearly before choosing what to do: would you be happy for me to give it to someone else?
ask just the question.
would you be happy for me to give it to someone else?
they say yes. write a short reply.
thank you. i will find someone who can use it.
a child draws a cloud over a house. does the picture tell us that it will rain at that house tomorrow?
no. a drawing is not information about tomorrow unless the story gives it that meaning. the cloud could simply be part of a picture the child wanted to make.
write a short story where the cloud is only there because the child likes drawing it.

a child draws a house and a large cloud above it. her father asks whether rain is coming. she says that she does not know the weather. she just likes the shape of the cloud and wanted one in her picture. then she puts a tree near the house and a small person by the door.
keep only the last sentence.
then she puts a tree near the house and a small person by the door.
does the small person have to be her father?
no. the story says a small person, but it does not say who the person is. the child could choose that detail later.
let it be the child herself. add one sentence.
she says that the person by the door is herself, coming home after school.
my brother and i went to the library together. he went inside, and i sat in the garden to draw. did we spend the whole visit together?
you went to the library together, then spent part of the visit in different places. you may have met again later, but that detail is not given.
answer simply.
you went there together, but then you were inside and outside in different places.
use just what i said, without changing who went inside.
you said he went inside while you sat in the garden. that part of the visit was not together.
write a story where we meet again before going home.

my brother and i went to the library together. he read inside while i drew in the garden. after a while, he came outside with his book. i showed him my picture, and he told me what he had read. then we walked home together.
what part did you add for the story?
i added that he came outside, you talked about the book and picture, and you walked home together. your first message did not give those later details.
is i has a book a good sentence?
use i have a book. with i, have is the correct choice here.
then can i say she have a book?
use she has a book. i have and she has are different in that way.
can you put both in a little conversation?
do you have a book? yes, i have a book. does your sister have one too? yes, she has one.
why did the question use have after does?
in a question with does, use have rather than has: does she have a book? in the answer, say she has a book.
now ask about both my sister and brother.
do your sister and brother have books?
yes, but i want to say they share one book rather than each having one.
then say: yes, they have one book that they share.
does that answer say i have the same book too?
no. it only says that your sister and brother share one. you would need another sentence to say whether you use it too.
my mother told a story about me as a child, but i remember one detail another way. i want to ask about it without saying the whole story is wrong.
you could say: i remember that part another way. can we talk about it? then give the specific detail you remember.
i remember another detail. can you say it simply?
then ask about that detail. you do not have to choose between saying every part is right and saying the whole story is wrong.
she says i had a red cup. i remember a blue cup from that time.
you could ask: was it the red cup on that day? i also remember a blue cup. could we be thinking of different days?
what if we do not have a picture to check?
you can leave the detail open. you both have a memory, but neither of you has to say you know more than you do.
make that idea simple.
you can say: we remember that part in a different way. we do not know for sure which cup it was.
can i still enjoy hearing the story?
yes. having a question about one cup does not have to take away the time you enjoy with your mother.
in my story, a woman sits down on a train and later gets off in a city. do i need to say how many hours the journey takes?
only if that detail helps the story you want to tell. you can tell what she sees or does without giving a number of hours.
answer simply.
no. you can tell the journey without giving a number of hours, unless the time is important to what happens next.
write a quiet journey with a book and a window.

a woman sits by the train window with a book. at first, she reads. then she closes it and looks at the town outside. she sees a garden, a long road, and people near a station. when the train stops in the city, she puts the book away and gets off.
keep only the sentence about closing the book.
then she closes the book and looks at the town outside.
did she finish the book?
no part of the story says that she finished it. she read for a while, looked outside, then put the book away.
make a last sentence saying she wants to read more later.
she keeps the book with her because she wants to read more after the visit.
if i use container as a general word, does it tell you whether it is open or closed?
no. container alone does not give that detail. it can be open, closed, large, small, full, or empty. other words can tell us which.
keep the answer simple.
no. container is general. you need other words to say whether it is open or closed.
i say the container is open and has three books inside. what do you know?
i know that it is open and that three books are inside. i do not know its color, whose it is, or where it is.
say only what you know.
it is open and has three books inside.
now i say it is on my desk. is the container mine for sure?
no. a container on your desk could still be something that another person has.
say that simply.
no. its place does not tell us whose it is.
give a short example.
your friend could leave a container on your desk. it would still be theirs.
my friend helped me find the right page before a reading. it was a small thing, but i want to thank them.
you could say: thank you for helping me find the page. it made starting the reading easy for me.
use easy in a shorter message.
thank you. your help made it easy to find the page.
can i say they helped with the whole reading?
that might sound as if they did more than find the page. keeping the thanks specific makes it clear what part they helped with.
make that answer simple.
say what they helped you do: find the page. that gives them thanks for the part they really did.
write it with no explanation after thank you.
thank you for helping me find the page.
now add that i was happy they were there, without saying i could not do it alone.
thank you for helping me find the page. i was happy you were there.
my brother says the room is full, and my sister says the table is empty. can they both be right?
yes. the room can have many people or things in it while the table has nothing on it. they are talking about different parts of the place.
write a short story where that happens during a family visit.

a family comes into a small room to talk. people sit on chairs and the sofa. a boy says that the room is full. his sister looks at the table, which has nothing on it yet, and says that it is empty. their mother asks her to bring the cups from the kitchen. soon the table has cups on it too.
did the room get larger when the table changed?
no. things were put on the table. the story does not say that the size of the room changed.
when would the two sentences give opposite information about the same thing?
if both people were talking about the same table at the same moment, saying it had nothing on it and saying it was full of cups would give opposite details.
ask my last question simply.
when would the two sentences give opposite information about the same thing?
write a story where a note answers one question but gives the person a new question.

a girl finds a book on the table and wants to know who brought it. inside is a note from her aunt saying that it is for her. now she knows who sent it, but she wants to know why her aunt chose that story. she calls her aunt and asks. her aunt says that it was a book she liked reading with the grandmother of the girl. the girl opens the first page and asks whether they can read it together on the next visit.
keep only the part about her aunt and grandmother reading together.
her aunt says that it was a book she liked reading with the grandmother of the girl.
what was the first question?
who brought or sent the book?
did the note say who carried it to the house?
the aunt gave the book, but another person could have carried it to the house. the note alone does not say who did that.
make that answer simple.
the aunt gave the book, but another person could have carried it to the house. the note alone does not say who did that.
add a sentence that makes her the person who brought it too.
the note says that her aunt left the book on the table during her visit that morning.
i wrote on one side of a piece of paper, then the other side. do i now have two pieces?
no. you have one piece with writing on one side and the other side. using the other side does not make another piece of paper.
say that with fewer words.
using the other side does not make another piece of paper. it is still one piece.
what if i cut it into two parts later?
if you cut one piece into two, you have two pieces. you did not add more paper.
say it simply.
if you cut one piece into two, you have two pieces. you did not add more paper.
can each piece have writing on it?
yes, if the writing is on both parts after the cut. the place of the writing and the number of pieces are different details.
give me a short example with one piece and writing on one side and a picture on the other.
i have one piece of paper. i wrote a message on one side and drew a picture on the other.
my friend wants to keep talking about a film, but i would like to talk about something else. i do not want to say the film is wrong to talk about.
you can ask to talk about something else without giving a reason about the film: could we talk about something else for a while?
use words we have in a request about my day.
you could say: could we talk about something else for a while? i would like to tell you about my day.
what if they ask whether i did not like the film?
if you liked it, say that. you can like the film and still want to talk about something else now.
answer simply.
if you liked it, say that. you can like the film and still want to talk about something else now.
i liked it. write the whole request.
i liked the film, but i would like to talk about something else for a while. can i tell you about my day?
does that call their choice wrong?
no. it says what you would like to talk about next, rather than saying they were wrong to talk about the film.
picoboi, help me write a message about a book.
who is the message for, and what do you want to say about the book?
for my cousin. i want to ask if they liked it.
you could write: did you enjoy the book?
should you add that we read it together?
only if you tell me that happened. a message about a book does not mean that both people read it together.
we did read it together last week. now add that.
did you enjoy the book we read together last week?
what if i say make it more kind?
i can make it sound more kind while keeping to the facts: did you enjoy the book we read together last week? i would like to hear what you thought of it.
do you know whether i enjoyed reading it?
no. you told me that you read together, but you did not say how you felt about it. i should ask rather than add a feeling for you.
say my request simply.
make the message sound more kind.
